title: David Dhawan's Last Film Just Opened. It's Exactly the Chaos You'd Expect.
excerpt: Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai is messy, loud, and unapologetically 90s. Varun Dhawan and two leading ladies give the king of Hindi comedy the farewell he wanted — if not the numbers.
body:
There's a particular kind of Bollywood film that smells like your uncle's living room in 1997. The hero is in over his head with two women. The comedy is broad. The misunderstandings are avoidable. The songs are catchy. And somewhere in the middle, there's a scene where everyone ends up in the same room and starts yelling.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=rFOdIv1jwhc

David Dhawan has made this film approximately forty-seven times. And now, at what is reportedly the final curtain call of a career that defined Hindi commercial cinema for two decades, he's made it once more — with his own son in the lead.

Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai released on June 5 to the kind of opening that tells you everything and nothing. ₹8.65 crore on Day 1, boosted by a 50 percent discount on BookMyShow. Another ₹7.50 crore on Saturday, flat as a chapati. Two-day total: ₹15 crore. The weekend is tracking toward ₹23–25 crore, which puts it squarely in the zone of Varun's last outing, Sunny Sanskari Ki Tulsi Kumari — a film nobody outside its opening weekend remembers.

The numbers are modest. The film doesn't care.

The Plot You Already Know

Varun Dhawan plays Jas, a man married to Bani (Mrunal Thakur), who wants a career before she wants a baby. He wants fatherhood now. The marriage fractures. A court gives them six months to think it over. Jas, with all the decision-making skills of a golden retriever, decamps to London and promptly falls for Preet (Pooja Hegde). Both women end up pregnant. Chaos, naturally, follows.

If you grew up watching Judwaa, Coolie No. 1, or Biwi No. 1, this is your comfort food. David Dhawan doesn't reinvent; he revisits. The comedy is physical, the timing is metronomic, and the emotional beats land with the subtlety of a Bollywood slap.

Critics are split. Some call it a "spectacular family entertainer." Others note it follows "a very common template." Both are right. This is a David Dhawan film. The template is the point.

A Career Worth Celebrating

Here's what the box office won't tell you: David Dhawan didn't just make comedies. He invented the grammar of Hindi comedy for an entire generation.

Before him, Bollywood comedy meant Mehmood mugging for the camera in a side role. Dhawan made comedy the main event. He gave Govinda a second life. He turned Salman Khan funny in Partner. He made Karisma Kapoor dance in Hero No. 1 like the film's budget depended on it — which it probably did.

For the Indian diaspora, these films weren't just entertainment. They were the DVDs your parents rented from the Indian grocery store. They were Saturday nights when the whole family watched something together without anyone checking their phone, because phones didn't do anything yet. Haseena Maan Jaayegi. Mujhse Shaadi Karogi. Maine Pyaar Kyun Kiya. Every title sounds like a question, and the answer was always: because David Dhawan directed it.

Varun Steps Into His Father's Frame

The father-son dynamic gives the film its only real gravity. Varun Dhawan has spent a decade trying to be taken seriously — Badlapur, October, Bhediya — while also being pulled back into the orbit of his father's brand of cinema. Here, he surrenders to it completely. He's loose, goofy, committed to the bit. The double-takes are hereditary.

Mrunal Thakur brings more texture than the script probably asked for. Her Bani is frustrated, ambitious, and genuinely funny — not just the wife waiting to forgive. Pooja Hegde, meanwhile, lights up the London sequences with the kind of effortless charm that makes you wish the writing gave her more to do.

The film's real problem isn't quality. It's timing. Rom-coms are struggling theatrically in the post-pandemic era. Audiences have been conditioned to wait eight weeks for the OTT drop. The 50 percent BookMyShow discount on opening day wasn't generosity — it was survival strategy. When you're competing with a free couch and JioHotstar, ₹200 off a ticket is the new floor price for getting people out of the house.

For the Diaspora: What You Need to Know

If you're in the US, UK, or Canada, Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai is playing in select multiplexes — expect it at your nearest Regal or Cineplex in metro areas with significant desi populations. The film is in Hindi with no dubbed versions.

For those waiting for streaming: given the ₹50–55 crore budget and current trajectory, an OTT window in 6–8 weeks is likely. JioHotstar or Netflix would be the probable home, though no deal has been announced.

"Now you can't stop anyone. Every producer thinks, 'Main kyun aage jaau?'" — Taran Adarsh, on the crowded June release calendar

David Dhawan is 71. He's made over 45 films. He never won a National Award, never got a retrospective at a film festival, and never once pretended to be making art. He made people laugh. For thirty years. In a country of a billion people, that might be the hardest thing to do.

If this is really goodbye, it's exactly the goodbye he'd choose: loud, colourful, slightly ridiculous, and impossible to ignore.

Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai is now playing in theatres across India and in select international markets.
